newsitem.title: USA: Next step in the mutual fund evolution - supermarkets.
newsitem.headline: Next step in the mutual fund evolution - supermarkets.

text.p: Mutual fund companies are hoping to emulate supermarkets -- providing investors with all their financial needs with one-stop shopping.

Mutual fund supermarkets -- where one fund family sells not only its own funds, but also those of other companies -- now account for 15 percent of the $4 trillion industry, according to Fidelity Investments Managing Director Roger Servison.

For the first time, Fidelity, the nation's largest mutual fund company with $538 billion in assets under management, expects to sell to retail investors more non-Fidelity funds than its own named funds, he said.
The reason: "The mutual fund supermarket is the next step in the evolution of mutual funds," Servison said.
Forrester Research analyst Michael Gazala credits Charles Schwab's OneSource account with bringing the concept of supermarkets to the mutual fund industry in 1992.

"Schwab is definitely the leader of the market," Gazala said. The San Francisco-based discount brokerage house, which just recently began offering its own mutual funds, began with $1.8 billion in assets under management in its OneSource programme. It now has $50 billion under management compared with Fidelity, which Servison said has about $20 billion in assets under management in its supermarket segment alone.

Gazala estimated that the mutual fund supermarkets, some of which allow investors to trade, download prospectuses and compare fund performances online, account for 1 percent to 2 percent of the market. He estimated that by the year 2000, such malls will account for up to 20 percent of the market.

"We see the supermarkets as the fastest growing segment of mutual fund distribution," said Hannah Grove, a spokeswoman for Funds Distribution, a firm that helps mutual funds distribute and market their products.
Fidelity's Servison is even more upbeat about the supermarket prospect, seeing it growing to 25 percent to 30 percent of the industry's business.

"It already accounts for 15 percent of the industry and that is just in the past five years. The banks' share is 10 percent to 12 percent...This simple product idea has brought in more business than several hundred banks with thousands of branches out there for about 10 years."
Jeffrey Lyons, senior vice president at Schwab, noted his company's OneSource programme has grown "at over 40 percent annually and we're looking for significant growth in the years to come."
Schwab offers some of Fidelity's funds, while Fidelity does not offer any of Schwab's. The relationship is a tense one between the two giants.

"The question is how many marketplaces do we need to have our funds in," Servison said. "Right now, we're in several marketplaces. Whether we stay there (Schwab) or not I think it is hard to tell...What's the value to me of doing business with somebody who is a potential competitor? As long as there's value there, we'll do it. But you're constantly evaluating these relationships."
Volume and technology seem to be the keys to becoming a successful mutual fund mall.

Servison said the supermarket concept presents a great opportunity for smaller funds by allowing the portfolio manager to concentrate on investing while the large overseeing mutual fund company takes care of all the back office work such as making trades between funds, sending out statements and prospectuses and answering investors' questions.
"It's very tricky to make a profit on it," Servison said. "You don't get that much revenue and there's a lot of expense in servicing these customers...each transaction costs money."

Generally, the funds pay the supermarket a 0.25 percent fee to take care of the back office work. But the fund gets access to people it wouldn't normally see big brokers get a wider range of products.

But Funds Distributor's Grove noted, "The mutual fund industry has reinvented itself and forced the onus of bearing costs onto the product manufacturers. In most scenarios, the funds absorb any start-up and maintenance fees...which leaves the investor free to buy without transaction-based fees and without the fear of eroding his account accumulation."
